q:
Sports drinks fill an entire aisle at most grocery stores, and sales in the United States topped $9 billion in 2023. A 20-ounce bottle of the leading brand contains 34 grams of sugar. In a 2021 survey, 58 percent of high school athletes said they drink sports drinks during practice. Registered dietitian Marcus Bell, who has advised college and professional teams for 20 years, put it plainly: "For anyone exercising less than an hour, sports drinks are a waste of money. Water is the smarter choice."

Which of the following statements from the article is an opinion?
o: A 20-ounce bottle of the leading brand contains 34 grams of sugar.
Sports drinks are a waste of money for anyone exercising less than an hour.
Fifty-eight percent of surveyed athletes said they drink sports drinks during practice.
Bell has advised college and professional teams for 20 years.
w: Calling a product "a waste of money" is a judgment of its value. Bell's long experience makes his view more credible, but an expert's judgment is still an opinion, not a fact.

n.0: Sugar content can be checked on the nutrition label, so it is a fact.
n.2: This reports the result of a survey. What the athletes said can be verified from the survey data, so it is a fact.
n.3: Bell's work history can be confirmed through the teams or his employment records, so it is a fact.

q:
The HomeCheck 300 blood pressure monitor takes a reading in about 40 seconds and stores up to 120 results for two users. It runs on four AA batteries or the included wall adapter. The large, backlit screen is easy to read, and the cuff fits upper arms from 9 to 17 inches around. HomeCheck monitors have been sold in pharmacies since 2016. At $49.99, the HomeCheck 300 is a bargain, and customers will love how simple it is to use.

Which of the following statements from the product description are opinions? Select all that apply.
o: Customers will love how simple it is to use.
It runs on four AA batteries or the included wall adapter.
The cuff fits upper arms from 9 to 17 inches around.
HomeCheck monitors have been sold in pharmacies since 2016.
At $49.99, the HomeCheck 300 is a bargain.
The large, backlit screen is easy to read.
w: "Easy to read," "a bargain" and "customers will love" are judgments or predictions about feelings that buyers could dispute. The screen being large and backlit and the price being $49.99 are checkable, but each sentence's main claim is a judgment, so all three are opinions.

n.1: The power options can be checked by examining the product, so this is a fact.
n.2: The cuff range is a measurement that can be confirmed, so this is a fact.
n.3: Sales history can be confirmed through company or pharmacy records, so this is a fact.

q:
In January, trained observers on the fourth-floor medical unit at Bayview Hospital recorded staff cleaning their hands at 412 of 520 required moments, a rate of 79 percent. In late January, the unit installed alcohol gel dispensers beside every bed. The February audit found a rate of 91 percent. The report's author concluded, "The bedside dispensers were the best purchase the hospital made all year."

Which of the following best describes the author's conclusion?
o: It is a fact, because it is based on the measured hand-hygiene rates.
It is an opinion, because it relies on percentages that may be rounded.
It is a fact, because trained observers collected the data for the report.
It is an opinion, because it ranks this purchase above all others.
w: The audit rates are facts, but deciding that the dispensers were "the best purchase" of the year is a value judgment that goes beyond the data. Interpreting statistics in this way produces an opinion.

n.0: Facts can support a conclusion without making it a fact. "Best purchase" compares the dispensers to every other purchase, which the data do not measure and which people could judge differently.
n.1: The label is right but the reason is wrong. Rounded percentages are still checkable facts; the statement is an opinion because of the judgment word "best."
n.2: Who collected the data affects how reliable the rates are; it does not turn the author's judgment about the purchase into a fact.

q:
Until this spring, residents of Carver County who needed mental health support after business hours had to call a regional hotline based two states away or go to an emergency room. Launched in April, the county's new 24-hour crisis line answered 3,800 calls in its first six months, and it is an overdue improvement for families who once waited days for help. The line is staffed by licensed counselors and costs callers nothing.

In the second sentence, which word or phrase makes the sentence a statement of opinion?
o: answered 3,800 calls
overdue
24-hour
new
w: "Overdue" judges that the service should have existed sooner. That is a value judgment others may not share, so it turns the sentence into an opinion. The other details can all be checked.

n.0: A call count can be confirmed from the line's records. A number inside a sentence does not decide whether the sentence is a fact or an opinion.
n.2: The line's hours of operation can be verified, so "24-hour" is factual.
n.3: "New" can be checked against the April launch date, so here it states a fact rather than a judgment.

q:
Gabriela Ruiz is drafting a letter to her city council about drinking water. Her first draft begins, "The city's tap water is unsafe to drink." Her teacher points out that this sentence is an opinion as written. She suggests that Gabriela open with a fact that council members could verify for themselves, and then state her own view in a later sentence, so that her argument rests on evidence rather than on feeling.

Which revision follows her teacher's advice?
o: Experts agree that the city's tap water is probably unsafe for young children.
In a 2023 city test, water from 12 homes had lead above the federal action level.
The city's tap water is far too risky for families with babies and young children.
The city's tap water tastes worse than the bottled water sold in local stores.
w: A dated test with a stated number of homes and a federal standard can be checked against the city's test records, so it is a verifiable fact.

n.0: "Probably" signals a judgment, and claiming that experts agree does not make a judgment a fact. Expert opinion is still opinion.
n.2: "Far too risky" is a judgment about how much risk is acceptable, so the revision is still an opinion.
n.3: Taste is a matter of personal judgment; "tastes worse" cannot be proven.

q:
The Harlan Medical History Museum reopened in May after an 18-month renovation. The building, which first opened in 1931, now has an elevator and wider doorways. The flu exhibit, a stunning achievement, displays nurses' letters from 1918. Admission is free on the first Sunday of each month. Visitors should plan at least two hours to see everything.

Which sentence from the passage contains both a fact and an opinion?
o: The flu exhibit, a stunning achievement, displays nurses' letters from 1918.
The building, which first opened in 1931, now has an elevator and wider doorways.
Visitors should plan at least two hours to see everything.
The museum reopened in May after an 18-month renovation.
w: That the exhibit displays nurses' letters from 1918 can be checked, so it is a fact. The phrase "a stunning achievement" is the writer's judgment. The sentence mixes the two.

n.1: The opening year and the building's features can be checked, so the sentence contains facts and no judgment.
n.2: "Should plan" is advice, so the sentence is an opinion, but it contains no separate checkable fact about the museum.
n.3: Both the reopening date and the length of the renovation can be confirmed, so the sentence is entirely factual.

q:
The Millbrook City Council voted 5 to 2 in June to spend $1.2 million on the River Walk Trail. Construction crews began clearing the route along the riverbank in August. When finished, the paved trail will be 3.4 miles long, according to the approved plans. Council member Dana Whitfield, who voted yes, told reporters, "This trail will draw thousands of new visitors and bring our downtown shops back to life."

Which of the following statements from the article is an opinion?
o: The trail will draw thousands of new visitors and revive downtown shops.
The approved plans call for a paved trail 3.4 miles long.
Construction crews began clearing the route along the riverbank in August.
The council voted 5 to 2 in June to spend $1.2 million on the River Walk Trail.
w: Whitfield is predicting future results and judging their effect on downtown. A prediction like this cannot be proven when it is made, and others may expect different results, so it is an opinion.

n.1: The planned length is written in the approved documents and can be checked now, so this is a fact about the plan, not a guess about the future.
n.2: The start of construction can be confirmed by records or observation, so this is a fact.
n.3: The vote count and amount are part of the public council record, so they are facts.

q:
Standing desks have become common in American offices. A 2019 study of 300 office workers found that those who used standing desks for six months reported less lower-back pain than those who did not. Standing desks cost between $250 and $700 at major office suppliers. Several workers in the study said they felt more alert in the afternoon. It is a well-established fact that a standing desk is the healthiest choice for any office.

Which of the following statements is an opinion, even though the author presents it as established?
o: Standing desks cost between $250 and $700 at major office suppliers.
Workers who used standing desks for six months reported less lower-back pain.
Several workers in the study said they felt more alert in the afternoon.
A standing desk is the healthiest choice for any office.
w: Calling something "the healthiest choice for any office" is a sweeping judgment. Labeling it "a well-established fact" does not make it one; the study supports a narrower finding about back pain, not a ranking of every option for every office.

n.0: Prices can be verified at the suppliers, so this is a fact.
n.1: This reports a study result that can be checked against the published study, so it is a fact.
n.2: "Felt more alert" describes a feeling, but the statement reports what workers said, which the study records can confirm. It is a fact about their reports.

q:
The city plans to build a five-story parking garage on the empty lot at Elm and Third Streets. The project would add 420 spaces and cost $11 million, paid for by a bond measure on the November ballot. City planners call the garage "badly needed" and say it would serve visitors to the hospital, the library and the new courthouse. Voters should see this money pit for what it is: a gift to downtown developers at the expense of ordinary taxpayers. Construction would take about 18 months.

Which phrase from the passage most clearly reveals the author's bias?
o: call the garage "badly needed"
paid for by a bond measure
this money pit
the empty lot at Elm and Third Streets
w: "Money pit" is loaded language: a negative label that pushes readers to see the garage as wasteful before any evidence is weighed. That emotional slant reveals the author's bias against the project.

n.0: "Badly needed" is a judgment, but it belongs to the city planners, whom the author quotes. Reporting another group's view is not the author's own slant, and the planners' view is the opposite of the author's.
n.1: This states how the project would be financed, a neutral and checkable detail.
n.3: "Empty lot" describes the site's current condition and can be checked; it carries no judgment.

q:
Mercy General Hospital's volunteer program has grown to 160 members this year. Volunteers greet visitors, deliver flowers and mail, and push wheelchairs from the lobby to patient units. Everyone must complete eight hours of training before working a first shift. The youngest volunteer is 16 and the oldest is 87. According to the program's sign-up records, most volunteers are retired. Older volunteers, of course, struggle with the new tablet check-in system, so the hospital pairs them with high school volunteers. Many volunteers say the work gives them a sense of purpose.

Which sentence from the passage contains a stereotype?
o: Older volunteers, of course, struggle with the new tablet check-in system.
The youngest volunteer is 16 and the oldest is 87.
According to the program's sign-up records, most volunteers are retired.
Many volunteers say the work gives them a sense of purpose.
w: The sentence treats all older volunteers as struggling with technology, and "of course" presents that as obvious. An oversimplified generalization about a whole group is a stereotype.

n.1: Two ages are reported as facts. Mentioning age is not the same as making a generalization about an age group.
n.2: This reports a share taken from the program's own records, which can be checked. A statement about most members of a group that rests on records is a statistic, not an assumed trait applied to everyone in the group.
n.3: This reports what volunteers themselves said. "Many" describes a share of real responses, not an assumption about a group's traits.

q:
Each winter, clinic phones ring with requests for antibiotics to treat colds. Many callers believe the drugs will help them get over a cold sooner. Colds, however, are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses. Taking antibiotics when they are not needed can cause side effects such as diarrhea and rashes, and it helps bacteria become resistant to the drugs. Rest, fluids and time remain the main treatment for most colds.

Which misconception does the passage seek to correct?
o: That antibiotics will help a person recover from a cold faster
That colds are caused by viruses rather than by bacteria
That antibiotics can cause side effects such as diarrhea and rashes
That rest and fluids are the main treatment for most colds
w: The passage reports the belief that antibiotics shorten a cold and then explains why it is wrong: antibiotics act on bacteria, and colds are viral. A commonly held but incorrect belief is a misconception.

n.1: This is the correct information the author uses to correct the misconception, not the misconception itself.
n.2: The author states this as a fact to show why unneeded antibiotics are harmful.
n.3: The author endorses this as the accurate treatment advice; it is not presented as a mistaken belief.

q:
A new study reports that adults who took VitaCore daily for 12 weeks had 30 percent fewer sick days than adults who took a placebo, or sugar pill. The study included 64 office workers in one city. It was paid for and run by VitaCore Nutrition, the company that sells the supplement, and its results have not been reviewed by outside scientists. VitaCore's website now calls the product "clinically proven to keep you healthy all year."

Which detail from the passage most strongly suggests that the study's findings may be biased?
o: The study compared the supplement with a placebo.
The study reported its main result as a percentage of sick days.
The study included 64 office workers from one city.
The supplement's seller paid for and ran the study.
w: A company that profits from the product has a financial interest in a favorable result. When the seller funds and runs its own study, the findings may be slanted toward the product, which is a classic source of bias.

n.0: A placebo comparison is a strength of study design; it helps rule out the effect of simply taking a pill.
n.1: Reporting a result as a percentage is a neutral way to present data and says nothing about whose interests the study serves.
n.2: A small, local sample makes the evidence less sufficient and harder to generalize, but that is a limitation of size, not a sign that the results were slanted toward one side.

q:
Critics have called the city's summer jobs program "a handout for kids who don't want to work." The numbers tell a different story. Last summer, 640 teenagers worked an average of 22 hours a week at parks, libraries and health clinics, and 91 percent of them completed the full eight weeks. Anyone who still sneers at these hardworking young people simply hasn't bothered to look at the facts.

Which phrase from the passage reveals the author's own bias?
o: worked an average of 22 hours a week at parks
91 percent of them completed the full eight weeks
a handout for kids who don't want to work
still sneers at these hardworking young people
w: "Sneers" casts the program's critics in a scornful light, and "hardworking young people" praises the teens with loaded, favorable wording. These are the author's own words, and they show a one-sided slant in favor of the program.

n.0: This is a checkable figure about hours worked, stated in neutral terms.
n.1: This is a checkable statistic about completion, stated in neutral terms.
n.2: These loaded words belong to the critics, whom the author quotes in order to argue against them. A view the author reports and refutes is not the author's own bias.

q:
Last week, the board of directors of Northfield Health announced a scheme to swallow up beloved St. Anne's Hospital. Under the merger, St. Anne's would keep its emergency department but close its maternity ward, and expectant mothers would travel 25 miles to Northfield's main campus. The board says the change will save $4 million a year. A public hearing is scheduled for March 12 at the county courthouse.

Which of the following words or phrases from the passage are examples of loaded language? Select all that apply.
o: swallow up
announced
scheme
merger
beloved
board of directors
w: "Scheme" suggests a sneaky plot, "swallow up" suggests a greedy takeover, and "beloved" adds warm emotion to one side. Each word carries a strong connotation that pushes the reader toward the author's view, which is what loaded language does.

n.1: "Announced" is a neutral verb for making information public.
n.3: "Merger" is the standard, neutral business term for two organizations combining.
n.5: "Board of directors" is the neutral name for the group that governs the company.

q:
The school board is considering two plans. Plan A, proposed by a group of parents and pediatricians, would move the high school start time from 7:20 to 8:30 a.m. Its supporters cite research showing that teenagers who start school later sleep more, miss fewer days and are involved in fewer car crashes. They note that districts in several states have made the change with strong results. Plan B, from the transportation office, would keep the current schedule to save on bus costs.

The author's bias is most evident in the way the passage
o: explains that the second plan would keep the current schedule to reduce bus costs.
states the exact current and proposed start times for the high school day.
supports one plan with detailed evidence but gives the other one sentence.
identifies the parents, pediatricians and transportation staff who proposed each plan.
w: Plan A gets research findings, several benefits and examples from other districts, while Plan B gets one sentence and no evidence. Unequal treatment of the two sides is a sign of bias, even when no single word is openly loaded.

n.0: Stating Plan B's purpose is fair to that side; the bias lies in how little support Plan B receives compared with Plan A.
n.1: The start times are neutral, checkable details.
n.3: Naming who proposed each plan is balanced; both sources are identified.

q:
A reporter for a local paper is revising a story about a zoning meeting. Her editor has asked her to describe both sides in neutral language so that readers can judge the issue for themselves. Her first draft includes this sentence:

The stubborn residents of Oak Street refused to budge on the cell tower, whining that it would ruin their views.

Which revision presents the residents' position without bias?
o: The residents of Oak Street opposed the cell tower, saying it would block their views.
The residents of Oak Street stubbornly opposed the cell tower, saying it would block their views.
The residents of Oak Street complained repeatedly that the cell tower would block their views.
The determined residents of Oak Street bravely stood against the tower to protect their views.
w: "Opposed" and "saying" report the residents' position and reason without judging them. The revision removes "stubborn," "refused to budge" and "whining," which all carried negative connotations.

n.1: "Stubbornly" keeps the negative judgment from the original draft.
n.2: "Complained repeatedly" still frames the residents as whiners, so the negative slant remains.
n.3: "Determined" and "bravely" replace a negative slant with a positive one. Bias in favor of a group is still bias.

q:
Dr. Lena Park, the economist who testified in favor of the proposed soda tax, presented data from two cities where soda purchases fell by about 20 percent after similar taxes took effect. But what would she know about the lives of working families? Dr. Park lives in a wealthy suburb, drives a luxury car and has probably never had to stretch a grocery budget. The council should reject this tax.

How does the author mainly attempt to discredit the case for the soda tax?
o: By questioning whether the two cities Dr. Park studied resemble this one
By attacking Dr. Park's personal life instead of responding to her data
By presenting data from other cities that contradict Dr. Park's findings
By explaining how the tax would raise grocery costs for working families
w: The author never addresses the 20 percent drop. Instead, the author points to where Dr. Park lives and what she drives. Attacking the person rather than the evidence (an ad hominem attack) is a sign of bias.

n.0: Questioning whether the cities are comparable would be a fair challenge to her evidence, but the author never raises it.
n.2: The author offers no data of any kind; the only figures in the passage are Dr. Park's.
n.3: The author mentions working families but never explains any effect of the tax on grocery costs; the focus stays on Dr. Park herself.

q:
The Main Street Farmers Market has operated every summer since 2018. Supporters say it has transformed downtown. In its best season, 2022, the market drew 48,000 visitors, and nearby shops reported their strongest summer sales in a decade. Vendors praise the friendly crowds and the shaded location along the river. Clearly, the market is a success that deserves a permanent city subsidy of $75,000 a year.

Which feature of the passage most strongly suggests a biased presentation?
o: It reports figures from the market's best year and omits the others.
It includes specific numbers about visitors and the size of the subsidy.
It states the author's conclusion in the final sentence of the passage.
It describes vendors' opinions about the crowds and the location.
w: The market has run for several seasons, yet the author reports figures from only its best one. Choosing the most favorable data while leaving out the rest (cherry-picking) gives a one-sided picture and signals bias.

n.1: Specific numbers can make a passage more balanced, not less. The problem is which numbers were chosen, not that numbers appear.
n.2: Placing a conclusion at the end is a structural choice that any writer, biased or not, might make.
n.3: Reporting what vendors say is a normal way to add detail; it does not by itself slant the presentation.

q:
Parents often warn children that reading in dim light will ruin their eyesight. Eye doctors say this belief is mistaken. Reading in poor light can make the eyes feel tired and dry and may bring on a headache, but these effects go away after rest and leave no lasting damage. Nearsightedness, which has become more common among children, is linked to family history and to spending little time outdoors.

Which statement would the author identify as a misconception?
o: Reading in dim light causes lasting harm to eyesight.
Eye strain from poor lighting goes away with rest.
Reading in dim light can make the eyes feel tired.
Nearsightedness is linked to spending little time outdoors.
w: The passage presents the warning that dim light "will ruin" eyesight as a widely held belief that eye doctors say is mistaken, because the effects are temporary. That makes it a misconception.

n.1: The author states this directly as fact to explain why no lasting damage occurs.
n.2: The author accepts this as true; tired, dry eyes are named as a real short-term effect.
n.3: The author presents this link as accurate information about the real causes of nearsightedness.

q:
The new QuickCare urgent care center on Route 9 is the best thing to happen to Fairview in years. Wait times average 15 minutes, the staff is friendly, and the building is spotless. The center accepts most major insurance plans and is open seven days a week from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. Families who have been driving 40 minutes to the county hospital for minor injuries finally have a better option close to home.

Which additional fact about the writer of this review would most strongly suggest that the review is biased?
o: The writer visited the center twice before writing the review.
The writer has written health columns for the paper for six years.
The writer lives about 2 miles from the new center.
The writer is a part owner of the QuickCare center.
w: A part owner profits when the center attracts patients. That financial interest gives the writer a reason to present the center favorably, which is an undisclosed interest and a strong sign of bias.

n.0: Visiting the center more than once is firsthand experience; it does not give the writer a stake in the outcome.
n.1: Years of experience writing health columns adds credibility and creates no conflict of interest.
n.2: Living nearby may explain the writer's interest in the center, but it gives no personal gain from praising it.

q:
After her knee replacement, Mrs. Tran was ambulatory by the second day; that is, she could make it to the end of the hallway and back with a cane for support. The physical therapist recorded her distance each afternoon and expected her to manage the stairs before the end of the week.

As used in the passage, the word ambulatory most nearly means
o: free of pain.
in need of an ambulance.
ready to go home.
able to walk.
w: The phrase "that is" introduces a restatement: she could make it down the hallway and back with a cane. Ambulatory means able to walk.

n.0: The passage says nothing about pain; walking with a cane does not tell us whether she still hurts.
n.1: "Ambulance" looks and sounds similar, but the passage describes her moving on her own, not being transported.
n.2: Discharge is not mentioned, and the therapist still expects more progress this week, so "ready to go home" goes beyond the clue.

q:
The two men admitted to Room 412 could not have been more different. Mr. Ortiz, who chatted with every nurse and shared stories about his grandchildren, made friends on the first day. Mr. Hale, by contrast, was reticent, answering most questions with a nod or a single word and turning toward the window when visitors arrived.

As used in the passage, the word reticent most nearly means
o: confused about his care.
unable to hear well.
reluctant to speak.
rude and unfriendly.
w: "By contrast" sets Mr. Hale against the talkative Mr. Ortiz, and the details (a nod, a single word) show someone who says little. Reticent means reluctant to speak or reserved.

n.0: His short answers show reserve, not confusion; the passage gives no sign that he misunderstands anything.
n.1: He responds to questions with a nod, which shows he hears them; the contrast is about talkativeness, not hearing.
n.3: Nothing shows hostility; he answers questions, just briefly. "Rude" adds a negative judgment the context does not support.

q:
Surgeons review each patient's full history before an operation. Patients with comorbidities, such as diabetes combined with high blood pressure or asthma combined with heart disease, often need longer recovery times and closer monitoring after surgery than patients who have only the condition being treated.

As used in the passage, the word comorbidities most nearly means
o: two or more conditions present at once.
conditions passed down within families.
illnesses that spread from patient to patient.
complications caused by the surgery itself.
w: The examples after "such as" each pair two conditions in one person, and the final phrase contrasts them with patients who have only one condition. Comorbidities are conditions that exist at the same time in the same patient.

n.1: None of the examples is described as inherited; the clue is that two conditions occur together.
n.2: Nothing in the examples involves contagion; diabetes and heart disease do not spread between patients.
n.3: The examples are conditions the patient already has before surgery, not problems the operation creates.

q:
Because cold, dry air can exacerbate asthma, the school nurse sent a note home before winter recess began. She advised students with asthma to wear a scarf over their mouths and noses outdoors and to keep their rescue inhalers with them, since coughing and wheezing tend to increase on the coldest days.

As used in the passage, the word exacerbate most nearly means
o: worsen.
relieve.
reveal.
cause.
w: The nurse's precautions and the note that symptoms "tend to increase" on cold days show that cold air makes existing asthma worse. Exacerbate means to worsen.

n.1: "Relieve" is the opposite; precautions would not be needed if cold air eased symptoms.
n.2: Nothing suggests cold air uncovers hidden asthma; the students and the nurse already know who has it.
n.3: The students already have asthma; cold air triggers more symptoms in an existing condition rather than creating the disease.

q:
The new scheduling plan was met with tepid support at the staff meeting. A few nurses nodded politely, but no one volunteered to help test it, and the sign-up sheet posted outside the break room stayed nearly empty for a week. The unit manager decided to delay the change until she could gather more feedback.

As used in the passage, the word tepid most nearly means
o: quiet but loyal.
openly hostile.
slightly warm.
unenthusiastic.
w: Polite nods, no volunteers and an empty sign-up sheet describe support that exists but lacks energy. Here tepid means unenthusiastic or halfhearted.

n.0: No one acts on the plan, so the context shows weak support, not loyalty.
n.1: No one objects or argues; polite nodding is the opposite of open hostility.
n.2: "Slightly warm" is the literal dictionary meaning, used for liquids; it does not fit support for a plan.

q:
When Jasmine opened the supply closet at the start of her shift, she found it in disarray. Rolls of gauze, boxes of gloves and packets of syringes were jumbled together on the same shelves, and nothing was where the labels said it would be. Every item on her restocking checklist was there, but it took her twenty minutes to sort everything back into place.

As used in the passage, the word disarray most nearly means
o: a shortage of supplies.
a state of disrepair.
a state of disorder.
an unsanitary condition.
w: "Jumbled together," "nothing was where the labels said" and the need to "sort everything back into place" all describe a mess. Disarray means disorder.

n.0: Every item on her checklist was there; the problem was where the supplies were, not how many there were.
n.1: "Disrepair" looks similar, but it means broken or damaged. Nothing in the closet is described as broken, and Jasmine fixes the problem by sorting, not repairing.
n.3: Nothing mentions dirt or contamination; the items are mixed up, not unclean.

q:
Teresa Ferreira has worked the night shift on the cardiac unit for eleven years, and she is meticulous about medication records. She double-checks every dose against the written order, initials each entry, and has never left a blank line on a chart. New graduates are often assigned to shadow her during their first week on the unit.

Which phrases from the passage help the reader determine the meaning of meticulous? Select all that apply.
o: double-checks every dose
has worked the night shift on the cardiac unit
for eleven years
initials each entry
New graduates are often assigned to shadow her
has never left a blank line on a chart
w: Meticulous means extremely careful about details. Double-checking every dose, initialing every entry and leaving no blank lines are examples of that careful attention, so they serve as example clues.

n.1: Her shift tells when she works, not how carefully she works.
n.2: Length of service shows experience; an experienced nurse is not necessarily a careful one.
n.4: New graduates shadowing her suggests she is respected, but it does not describe the quality the word names; the reason for the assignment is not stated.

q:
Ms. Bryant reacted to both antibiotics, but in very different ways. Whereas the first drug produced a transient rash that faded within a few hours, the second caused hives that lasted for several days and required a visit to an allergist. Her chart now lists the second drug as an allergy.

As used in the passage, the word transient most nearly means
o: covering a wide area.
visible.
short-lived.
delayed.
w: "Whereas" signals a contrast between a rash that "faded within a few hours" and hives that "lasted for several days." The contrast is about duration, so transient means short-lived.

n.0: The passage says nothing about how much of her body the rash covered; the contrast is about how long each reaction lasted.
n.1: Both the rash and the hives were visible, so "visible" cannot be the point of the contrast.
n.3: "Delayed" concerns when a reaction starts, but the clue describes how quickly the rash went away.

q:
By early morning the river had risen eight feet, and rain was still falling across the valley. Emergency managers warned that flooding of the lower streets was imminent: water was expected to spill over the riverbank within hours. They urged residents of those streets to leave their homes by noon and opened two shelters on higher ground.

As used in the passage, the word imminent most nearly means
o: severe and damaging.
about to happen.
widely respected.
unlikely but possible.
w: The colon introduces a restatement: water was "expected to spill over the riverbank within hours." Imminent means about to happen.

n.0: The restatement after the colon is about timing (within hours), not about how much damage the flood would do.
n.2: "Widely respected" is the meaning of eminent, a look-alike word that does not fit a flood warning.
n.3: Officials opened shelters and set a noon deadline, which shows they expected the flood soon, not that it was unlikely.

q:
Twenty years ago, hand sanitizer was found mainly in hospitals and doctors' offices. Today it is ubiquitous: bottles sit on grocery checkout counters, hang from children's backpacks and stand beside the doors of nearly every school, gym and office building. Some health experts now remind the public that washing with soap and water remains the better choice when hands are visibly dirty.

As used in the passage, the word ubiquitous most nearly means
o: found almost everywhere.
required by law in public places.
highly effective against germs.
sold at a low price.
w: The colon introduces a list of places where sanitizer now appears: stores, backpacks, schools, gyms and offices. Ubiquitous means present almost everywhere.

n.1: No rule or law is mentioned; the list shows how common sanitizer is, not that it is mandatory.
n.2: The passage does not praise sanitizer's effectiveness; in fact it notes that soap and water are better in some cases.
n.3: Price is never mentioned in the passage.

q:
Because the medication can harm a developing fetus, it is contraindicated during pregnancy. For this reason, pharmacists ask every patient of childbearing age whether she might be pregnant before filling the prescription, and the label carries a bold warning on the front of the bottle.

As used in the passage, the word contraindicated most nearly means
o: prescribed at a lower dose than usual.
required by the prescriber.
less effective during pregnancy.
advised against because of risk.
w: "Because" links the harm to a fetus with the word, and the pharmacist's screening and bold warning show the drug should not be used in pregnancy. Contraindicated means advised against because it may cause harm.

n.0: A lower dose would still mean using the drug; the warnings and screening point to avoiding it.
n.1: This is close to the opposite; the context describes steps taken to keep pregnant patients from receiving the drug.
n.2: The concern in the passage is harm to the fetus, not whether the drug works less well.

q:
The safety committee's report was succinct. In just two pages, it summarized six months of meetings, listed three recommendations and set a deadline for each. Board members, who were used to reports of fifty pages or more, praised the committee for its clarity and approved all three recommendations at the same meeting.

As used in the passage, the word succinct most nearly means
o: brief and to the point.
carefully and thoroughly researched.
easy to understand.
strongly worded.
w: "In just two pages" and the contrast with reports of "fifty pages or more" point to length. Succinct means brief and to the point.

n.1: Six months of meetings shows effort, but the clues next to succinct describe how short the report was, not how it was researched.
n.2: This matches a nearby word, "clarity," which describes a separate quality the board praised. The clues tied to succinct are about length.
n.3: Nothing describes the tone of the recommendations; the passage focuses on the report's length.

q:
Charge nurse Angela Morris is writing an annual review for Kayla Brooks, a nurse on her unit. When a patient's pain medication is late or a test result is missing, Kayla calls the pharmacy or the lab again and again until the problem is solved. Angela wants the review to praise this habit. She drafts the sentence, "Kayla is ______ when she advocates for her patients."

Which word best completes the sentence in a way that matches Angela's purpose?
o: obstinate
nagging
pushy
tenacious
w: All four words describe someone who keeps pressing, so their denotations overlap. Only "tenacious" carries a positive connotation (admirably determined), which fits a sentence meant to praise.

n.0: "Obstinate" suggests unreasonable stubbornness, a negative connotation that would criticize rather than praise.
n.1: "Nagging" suggests annoying, repeated complaining, which is negative.
n.2: "Pushy" describes the same behavior with a negative connotation of being rude or overbearing.

q:
I still remember Sunday mornings in my grandmother's kitchen: the radio playing gospel music, the smell of biscuits and coffee, and the yellow curtains she sewed herself. My cousins and I would crowd around the table while she told stories about growing up in Georgia. Grandma is ninety now and lives in a bright apartment near my parents, but whenever I smell fresh biscuits, I am eight years old again, waiting for the first one to cool.

Which word best describes the tone of the passage?
o: mournful
indifferent
humorous
nostalgic
w: The author recalls a cherished past with warm sensory details and a longing to return to it ("I am eight years old again"). A fond, wistful attitude toward the past is a nostalgic tone.

n.0: "Mournful" suggests grief over a loss. The grandmother is alive and well, and the memories are warm rather than sad.
n.1: "Indifferent" means not caring, but the vivid, affectionate details show the author cares deeply.
n.2: The passage is warm, not joking; no detail is meant to make the reader laugh.

q:
The Westside Free Clinic runs on a modest budget. Its two exam rooms share a single blood pressure machine, and most of the staff are volunteers who give one evening a week. Even so, the clinic saw more than 2,000 patients last year, and its director, Dr. Samuel Price, hopes to add a dental chair next spring if a local foundation approves his grant request.

The author describes the clinic's budget as "modest" rather than "meager." What is the effect of this word choice?
o: It suggests that the budget is too small to run the clinic.
It presents the small budget in a respectful light.
It suggests that the budget has grown since last year.
It makes the dollar amount of the budget more precise.
w: Both words mean small (similar denotation). "Modest" has a neutral-to-positive connotation of simple and unpretentious, while "meager" suggests a pitiful shortage. The choice frames the clinic with respect, which fits the author's admiring account of what it achieves.

n.0: That is the connotation of "meager," the word the author avoided; the passage stresses what the clinic accomplishes despite its size.
n.2: Neither word refers to change over time; the passage gives no information about last year's budget.
n.3: Neither word states an amount; the choice affects the feeling of the description, not its precision.

q:
Council member Ray Delgado has served the Third Ward for twelve years. Supporters call him resourceful, pointing to the new library he funded by combining three small state grants. His critics see a crafty politician who trades favors behind closed doors. Both sides agree that he is experienced and practical, and few people expect anyone to challenge him in the next election.

Which word from the passage carries a negative connotation?
o: resourceful
crafty
practical
experienced
w: "Crafty" means clever, but it suggests cunning or sneaky behavior. The critics use it alongside "trades favors behind closed doors," which confirms the negative connotation.

n.0: "Resourceful" also means clever at solving problems, but it carries a positive connotation; supporters use it as praise.
n.2: "Practical" is neutral to positive, suggesting sensible, realistic choices.
n.3: "Experienced" is neutral to positive; both sides use it as a fair description.

q:
The company claims its new wristband can detect dehydration before the wearer feels thirsty. Perhaps it can. But the company has not released any test data, and the two reviewers who wore the device during the same workout got readings that differed by 30 percent. Until an independent lab checks these claims, I would hold off on spending $199 for one. I'll believe it when I see the numbers.

Which word best describes the author's tone?
o: hostile
cynical
pessimistic
skeptical
w: The author doubts the claim but stays open to evidence ("Perhaps it can," "I'll believe it when I see the numbers"). Doubt that waits for proof is a skeptical tone.

n.0: "Hostile" suggests anger or attack; the author's language is measured and practical.
n.1: A cynical writer distrusts people's motives and assumes the worst. This author does not accuse the company of lying and allows that the device might work.
n.2: "Pessimistic" means expecting a bad outcome. The author withholds judgment until data arrive instead of predicting failure.

q:
After 34 years at Riverside Hospital, Nurse Paulette Greene retired last Friday. Former students lined the hallway to thank her. Many said they still hear her voice when they check an IV line. She was famous for her candid feedback: if a student's technique was wrong, she said so plainly, then stayed until the student got it right. "She told me the truth when I needed it most," one former student said.

Which word could replace candid without changing the author's admiring tone?
o: tactless
honest
brutal
blunt
w: "Honest" keeps both the meaning (saying things plainly and truthfully) and the positive connotation that fits an admiring tribute.

n.0: "Tactless" means insensitive to others' feelings, a clearly negative connotation that clashes with the praise.
n.2: "Brutal" suggests harshness or cruelty, which contradicts the patient teacher who stayed until students succeeded.
n.3: "Blunt" shares the meaning of speaking plainly, but it suggests abruptness or lack of tact, which would add a critical edge to the tribute.

q:
Ever since the new neighbor moved in, Mrs. Abbott has watched him from behind her curtains. "He's a scrawny young man," she told her sister, "and nosy, too. He asked me how long I'd lived here." Her sister laughed. "He sounds curious and friendly to me. And didn't you say he was lean and fit, out jogging every morning?" Mrs. Abbott frowned. "He rides that bicycle like a reckless child." Her sister shrugged. "Or like an adventurous one."

Which words from the passage carry a negative connotation? Select all that apply.
o: adventurous
curious
lean
reckless
scrawny
nosy
w: Mrs. Abbott chooses words with negative connotations: "scrawny" (unhealthily thin), "nosy" (intrusive) and "reckless" (dangerously careless). Her sister describes the same traits with positive words.

n.0: "Adventurous" describes the same willingness to take risks as "reckless" but suggests an appealing love of excitement, a positive connotation.
n.1: "Curious" names the same interest in others as "nosy" but with a positive connotation of healthy interest.
n.2: "Lean" describes the same thin build as "scrawny" but suggests fitness, a positive connotation.

q:
Last month, Lakeside Medical Center raised its parking fee for visitors to $28 a day. Families sitting at the bedsides of seriously ill loved ones, many of whom visit every day for weeks, now pay more than $800 a month simply to be present. The hospital made the change without a single public notice. This is an outrage, and the board owes these families an explanation and a refund.

Which word best describes the author's tone toward the hospital's decision?
o: resigned
indignant
sympathetic
sarcastic
w: "An outrage" and the demand for an explanation and a refund express anger at something the author considers unjust. Angry protest at an unfair act is an indignant tone.

n.0: "Resigned" means accepting something unwelcome as unavoidable, but the author demands that the board act.
n.2: The author does show sympathy, but toward the families. The question asks about the tone toward the hospital's decision, which is angry, not sympathetic.
n.3: Sarcasm says the opposite of what is meant; the author states the complaint directly.

q:
In a report on a hospital's new staffing model, the author writes: "Letting nurses design their own schedules through a shared online calendar is a bold experiment, and early results are encouraging. Overtime fell by 18 percent in the first quarter, and fewer nurses left the unit."

By calling the staffing model "a bold experiment," the author suggests that the model is
o: a daring new approach that deserves credit.
a careless gamble with nurses' schedules.
a proven method that other units already use.
a costly plan that the hospital should reconsider.
w: "Bold" carries a positive connotation of admirable daring, and "experiment" marks the model as new and untested. Together with "early results are encouraging," the word choice presents the model as a risk worth praising.

n.1: "Careless gamble" gives risk-taking a negative connotation. The author calls the results "encouraging," so the attitude is approving, not critical.
n.2: "Experiment" and "early results" show the model is new and still being tested, so it is not presented as proven or borrowed from other units.
n.3: The passage reports falling overtime and fewer nurses leaving and raises no cost concern, so nothing suggests the hospital should reconsider.

q:
Starting March 1, the county health department will require all restaurant employees who handle food to complete a two-hour safety course. The course is offered online and in person, costs $15 and covers handwashing, safe cooking temperatures and food storage.

Restaurant owners, do not wait. Classes are already filling up, and any employee without a certificate after March 1 will be barred from the kitchen. Sign your staff up today.

Which of the following best describes how the tone changes from the first paragraph to the second?
o: It moves from humorous to serious.
It moves from optimistic to pessimistic.
It moves from critical to celebratory.
It moves from objective to urgent.
w: The first paragraph reports the rule's details neutrally. The second uses commands ("do not wait," "sign your staff up today") and a warning about filling classes, which creates urgency.

n.0: The first paragraph contains no humor; it lists dates, costs and topics.
n.1: Neither paragraph expresses hope or gloom about the outcome; the second paragraph pushes for quick action rather than predicting a bad result.
n.2: Neither paragraph criticizes the rule or celebrates it; the shift is from reporting to pressing for action.

q:
A copywriter is preparing an advertisement for a discount pharmacy. Her first draft calls the store's generic vitamins "inexpensive." Her manager asks her to look for a word that means the same thing as inexpensive but that shoppers might read as an insult to the product's quality, so that she can be sure to avoid it in the final version.

Which word should the copywriter avoid?
o: shoddy
low-cost
cheap
affordable
w: "Cheap" shares the denotation of low price but often suggests poor quality, a negative connotation the manager wants to avoid.

n.0: "Shoddy" does insult the product's quality, but it means badly made, not low in price. It fails the manager's first test: it does not mean the same thing as inexpensive.
n.1: "Low-cost" states the low price in neutral terms and suggests nothing about quality.
n.3: "Affordable" means low in price with a positive connotation of good value, so it would not insult the product.

q:
To: Billing Department Staff
Subject: Forms (again)

As I have now explained at three separate meetings, completed insurance forms go in the blue tray, not the red one. I realize this may be a lot for some of you to keep track of, so I have taped a large, colorful sign above each tray with an arrow pointing to the right one. If anyone is still unsure, please feel free to stop by my office, and I will walk you through it slowly.

Which word best describes the tone of the memo?
o: lighthearted
accommodating
condescending
apologetic
w: Phrases such as "a lot for some of you to keep track of," the "large, colorful sign" and "walk you through it slowly" suggest the staff cannot handle a simple task. Talking down to the reader is a condescending tone.

n.0: The memo is not playful or trying to amuse; its mockery is aimed at the staff's abilities.
n.1: The offer of help looks accommodating on the surface, but "(again)," "three separate meetings" and "slowly" show irritation and talking down, not a genuine wish to help.
n.3: The writer apologizes for nothing; the memo places the blame on the staff.

q:
By 9 p.m. on Saturday, the emergency room was a beehive. Nurses moved quickly from bay to bay, phones rang at the front desk, and a steady line of patients waited to be checked in. Dr. Imani Carter, working her fourth night in a row, kept a list of every patient on a clipboard so that no one would be missed.

The phrase "the emergency room was a beehive" is an example of which of the following?
o: personification
simile
hyperbole
metaphor
w: The sentence says the room "was" a beehive, comparing the busy room to a hive directly, without "like" or "as." A direct comparison of this kind is a metaphor.

n.0: Personification gives human traits to something non-human. The room is compared to a hive; it is not given human actions or feelings.
n.1: A simile makes the comparison with "like" or "as" ("busy as a beehive"); this sentence has neither word.
n.2: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration. The comparison conveys the busy activity, which the details show is accurate rather than overstated.

q:
The research team had spent four months collecting blood samples from 200 volunteers. Then, during a power outage, the freezer that stored the samples failed overnight, and every sample was ruined. When the lead researcher, Dr. Kim, called the team together the next morning, she admitted that they were back to square one. Within a week, the team had begun recruiting new volunteers.

As used in the passage, the phrase "back to square one" means that the team was
o: returned to its original laboratory.
forced to start the work over.
waiting for the power to return.
blamed for losing the samples.
w: The idiom means having to start again from the beginning. The ruined samples and the team's decision to recruit new volunteers confirm that the work had to restart.

n.0: This reads the idiom literally as a place; the passage never mentions the team moving anywhere.
n.2: The outage had already happened; the idiom describes the loss of progress, not a wait for power.
n.3: No one is blamed; the freezer failed during a power outage.

q:
On the third day after surgery, the nurse removed Mr. Osei's bandage and checked the incision. The edges had closed, the surrounding skin was only slightly pink, and there was no discharge on the gauze. She recorded that the wound was healing well and told him that the stitches could come out at his follow-up visit.

As used in the passage, the word discharge most nearly means
o: a gap between the edges of a cut.
official release from the hospital.
redness of the skin around a wound.
fluid released from a wound.
w: The nurse is examining the gauze over an incision, so the word refers to fluid such as pus or blood coming from the wound. Its absence is a sign of healing.

n.0: The passage says separately that the edges had closed. A gap in the incision is not something that would appear on the gauze.
n.1: Release from the hospital is the most common meaning in a hospital setting, but the word here describes something that would appear on gauze.
n.2: The passage describes the skin's color separately ("only slightly pink"); discharge is something found on the gauze, not a color of the skin.

q:
The night shift on 6 North began quietly. A cold rain streaked the windows, and the hallway lights hummed overhead. At the nurses' station, an old coffee maker grumbled its way through one more pot. By midnight, the call lights were blinking at a steady pace, and Nurse Diaz had already walked what felt like ten miles.

Which phrase from the passage is an example of personification?
o: the hallway lights hummed overhead
walked what felt like ten miles
grumbled its way through one more pot
the call lights were blinking at a steady pace
w: To grumble is a human action (complaining in a low, irritated voice). Giving the coffee maker this human behavior is personification.

n.0: Lights and machines literally hum; this describes a real sound, not a human action.
n.1: This is hyperbole, an exaggeration of how far she walked, not a human trait given to an object.
n.3: Call lights really do blink; this is a literal description of the signals, not a human trait given to an object.

q:
Journal entry, week one of clinical rotations: By the end of my first twelve-hour shift, my feet weighed a thousand pounds. I had taken vital signs on eleven patients, helped turn a man who had just come out of surgery, and answered more call lights than I could count. I sat in my car in the parking garage for twenty minutes before I had the energy to drive home.

The author most likely writes that her feet "weighed a thousand pounds" in order to
o: show that she worked longer than planned.
emphasize how exhausted she felt.
compare nursing with heavy lifting work.
describe swelling caused by an injury.
w: The statement is hyperbole, a deliberate exaggeration. Together with sitting in the car for twenty minutes before she could drive, it emphasizes extreme tiredness.

n.0: The shift is described as twelve hours with no sign that it ran over; the phrase is about how she felt, not about the schedule.
n.2: She does turn a patient, but the phrase describes her own fatigue rather than comparing nursing to another job.
n.3: This reads the exaggeration literally; nothing in the entry describes an injury.

q:
The storm had knocked out the power for the third time that afternoon. Water was dripping from a crack in the kitchen ceiling into a row of mixing bowls, the basement was flooding, and the phone battery was at four percent. Marcus looked around the dark, damp room, sighed, and said to his sister, "Well, this is turning out to be a relaxing weekend."

Marcus's statement is an example of which of the following?
o: hyperbole
verbal irony
personification
situational irony
w: Marcus says the weekend is "relaxing" when he means the opposite. Saying one thing while meaning its opposite is verbal irony.

n.0: Hyperbole exaggerates the truth; Marcus reverses the truth rather than overstating it.
n.2: Marcus gives no human traits to an object; he comments on his own weekend.
n.3: Situational irony is an outcome that is the opposite of what is expected. The storm is unfortunate, but the irony here lies in Marcus's words, not in an unexpected outcome.

q:
In October, a regional pharmacy chain launched a campaign urging customers to get their flu shots early. The company hired a well-known local news anchor to appear in its ads, which showed her smiling as she rolled up her sleeve. On the day the campaign was set to launch, the anchor was unable to attend the kickoff event. She was home in bed with the flu.

Which of the following best describes the final two sentences of the passage?
o: They foreshadow a later event by hinting at what will happen to the campaign.
They create dramatic irony, because the reader knows something the anchor does not.
They create situational irony, because the outcome contradicts expectations.
They create verbal irony, because the anchor says the opposite of what she means.
w: The face of a campaign to prevent flu catches the flu on launch day. An outcome that contradicts what the situation leads us to expect is situational irony.

n.0: The passage ends with the outcome; it hints at no future event, so this is not foreshadowing.
n.1: Dramatic irony requires the reader to know something a character does not; here the reader learns about the flu at the same moment as the outcome is revealed.
n.3: The anchor says nothing in the passage, so there are no words that could mean the opposite of their literal sense.

q:
Ms. Patel came to the clinic with a sore throat and a fever of 101.8 degrees. The nurse practitioner swabbed the back of her throat and explained that the lab would culture the sample to see whether strep bacteria were present. Results would be ready in about 48 hours, and Ms. Patel was asked to rest at home until then.

As used in the passage, the word culture most nearly means
o: study the customs of a group.
grow microorganisms for testing.
kill germs on equipment and surfaces.
improve through education.
w: The lab is checking whether bacteria are present in a throat sample, and results take 48 hours. In this context, to culture means to grow microorganisms from a sample so they can be identified.

n.0: This is the most common meaning of culture (the customs and arts of a people), but it does not fit a lab testing a throat swab.
n.2: Killing germs is the opposite of what the lab needs; it wants any bacteria in the sample to grow so they can be identified.
n.3: "Cultured" can describe a person refined by education, a meaning unrelated to a lab sample.

q:
Monday mornings in the hospital admissions office are organized chaos. The phones ring nonstop, and the line at the front desk stretches like a ribbon to the main doors. Clerks wade through a sea of paperwork while the old printer in the corner coughs out one form after another. Somehow, every patient is registered by noon.

Which phrase from the passage is an oxymoron?
o: organized chaos
a sea of paperwork
stretches like a ribbon
coughs out one form
w: An oxymoron joins two words with opposite meanings. "Organized" and "chaos" contradict each other, and together they capture an office that is busy and messy yet still gets the job done.

n.1: This is a metaphor: it calls a large amount of paperwork a sea without using "like" or "as."
n.2: This is a simile: it compares the line to a ribbon using "like."
n.3: This is personification: coughing is a human action given to a printer.

q:
The hospital spent $2 million on new records software last year, and nurses were promised faster access to patient information. Instead, finding a single lab result now takes six clicks and two passwords, and the system logs users out after five minutes. For the nurses on the night shift, the new software has become a locked door between them and their patients.

In the final sentence, the author's description of the software as "a locked door" suggests that the software
o: keeps patient records more secure than before.
is closed to nurses who work the night shift.
blocks nurses from the information they need.
physically separates the nurses' station from rooms.
w: The details before the metaphor (six clicks, two passwords, frequent logouts) show nurses struggling to reach patient information. The "locked door" stands for that barrier.

n.0: Locks can suggest security, but the passage criticizes the software for slowing nurses down; it never praises its protection of records.
n.1: Night-shift nurses are mentioned as the group most affected, but they can still use the system; the passage describes difficulty, not a ban.
n.3: This reads the metaphor literally; the software is not a physical barrier between rooms.

q:
Read the sentences from a short story set in a pediatric clinic.

Her laugh rang out like a bell across the waiting room. By noon, the waiting room was an oven. The toddler was as restless as a puppy in a bathtub. Parents who would like a blanket for their child can ask at the desk. The old radiator groaned and complained all morning. The receptionist moved through the crowd like a seasoned conductor.

Which of the following sentences contain a simile? Select all that apply.
o: The toddler was as restless as a puppy in a bathtub.
Parents who would like a blanket for their child can ask at the desk.
The old radiator groaned and complained all morning.
By noon, the waiting room was an oven.
Her laugh rang out like a bell across the waiting room.
The receptionist moved through the crowd like a seasoned conductor.
w: A simile compares two unlike things using "like" or "as." The laugh is compared to a bell, the toddler to a puppy, and the receptionist to a conductor.

n.1: "Would like" means "want"; the word "like" here makes no comparison.
n.2: Groaning and complaining are human actions given to a radiator, which is personification.
n.3: This compares the room to an oven directly, without "like" or "as," so it is a metaphor.

q:
Hurricane Delia tore across Port Ellis last weekend with winds of 120 miles per hour. It ripped the roofs from more than half of the town's homes, flooded the only bridge to the mainland and left 9,000 residents without power. At a press conference on Monday, Mayor Teresa Ruiz looked at the crowd of reporters and said, "We've had a bit of a rough week."

The mayor's statement is an example of which of the following?
o: understatement
allusion
hyperbole
personification
w: Calling a devastating hurricane "a bit of a rough week" makes the situation sound far less serious than it is. Deliberately downplaying something is understatement.

n.1: An allusion refers to a well-known person, place, event or work; the mayor refers to none.
n.2: Hyperbole is the opposite: exaggerating to make something seem bigger. The mayor makes the disaster sound smaller.
n.3: Personification gives human traits to a non-human thing; the mayor describes the town's week without giving any object human qualities.

q:
To the Bellmont City Council:

Every school morning, about 300 students cross Route 6 to reach Lincoln Elementary. The road has no crosswalk within half a mile of the school, and cars there travel at an average of 41 miles per hour, according to the county's own traffic study. Last year, police recorded four collisions involving pedestrians on that stretch. A marked crosswalk with flashing lights would cost about $60,000, less than the city spent repaving the parking lot at City Hall. I urge you to fund it at your next meeting.

What is the author's primary purpose in this letter?
o: to describe the morning walk that students take to school
to persuade the council to install a crosswalk near the school
to inform readers about the county's traffic study on Route 6
to criticize the council for repaving the City Hall parking lot
w: The letter closes with a direct request ("I urge you to fund it"), and each fact is chosen to support that request. Facts that serve a claim make the purpose persuasive, not informative.

n.0: The students' crossing is mentioned to show the danger, not described in detail.
n.2: The traffic study is used as evidence for the request; the letter does not explain the study for its own sake.
n.3: The parking lot comparison is a single supporting point used to show the crosswalk is affordable; it is not the main aim of the letter.

q:
Most vaccines must be kept between 36 and 46 degrees Fahrenheit from the moment they leave the factory until they are given to a patient. This unbroken chain of refrigeration is called the cold chain. Vaccines travel in insulated containers with temperature monitors, and clinics store them in refrigerators that record the temperature every few minutes. If a reading falls outside the safe range, staff label the vaccines "do not use" and contact the state health department, which decides whether the doses can still be given.

What is the primary purpose of the passage?
o: to persuade readers to receive recommended vaccines
to explain how vaccines are kept safely cold
to criticize clinics that store vaccines incorrectly
to describe the history of vaccine refrigeration
w: The passage defines the cold chain and walks through how vaccines are shipped, stored, monitored and handled when a problem occurs. Its neutral, step-by-step explanation shows an informative purpose.

n.0: The topic is vaccines, but the passage never urges anyone to be vaccinated. Confusing the topic with the purpose leads to this choice.
n.2: The passage describes what staff do when temperatures go out of range; it does not fault any clinic.
n.3: No dates or past developments are given; the passage describes current practice.

q:
Our beagle, Biscuit, has never once come when called. But on Thanksgiving, as my uncle set the turkey on the counter and turned to find the carving knife, Biscuit materialized like a furry magician. By the time my uncle turned back, the turkey was gone, and so was the dog. We found them both under my parents' bed twenty minutes later: Biscuit asleep with his paws around a drumstick, looking prouder than any dog has a right to look. We had pizza for dinner. Biscuit had nothing to eat for the rest of the day, and he did not seem to mind.

What is the author's primary purpose in this passage?
o: to explain how to prepare a holiday meal for a large family
to entertain readers with a funny story about a family dog
to persuade readers to keep food out of a dog's reach
to inform readers about why beagles are hard to train
w: The passage tells a story with comic details (the "furry magician," the proud dog hugging a drumstick, pizza for Thanksgiving dinner) and makes no argument or lesson. Its purpose is to entertain.

n.0: The holiday meal is the setting of the story, not a set of instructions.
n.2: A reader might draw this lesson, but the author never urges it; the story is told for amusement.
n.3: The author mentions that Biscuit never comes when called, but offers no information about beagles as a breed or about training.

q:
When Rosa Jimenez, 58, felt a sudden ache in her jaw while gardening, she assumed she had pulled a muscle. Two hours later, she was in a cardiac unit. Rosa's experience is common. Women having a heart attack often notice symptoms other than chest pain, such as jaw or back pain, nausea, shortness of breath or unusual fatigue. Because these symptoms are less familiar, women often wait longer than men before seeking care. Doctors advise anyone with these symptoms to call 911 rather than drive to the hospital.

Why does the author most likely begin the passage with Rosa Jimenez's experience?
o: to show that jaw pain is the most common symptom in women
to entertain readers with a dramatic story
to draw readers in with a real example of the problem
to argue that gardening is risky for older adults
w: The anecdote puts a human face on the problem the passage goes on to explain: women's heart attack symptoms are often missed. An opening story in an informational text usually serves to engage the reader and introduce the topic.

n.0: Jaw pain is listed as one of several possible symptoms; the passage does not rank it as the most common.
n.1: The story is dramatic, but it introduces factual health information; the passage as a whole informs rather than entertains.
n.3: Gardening is simply what Rosa was doing; the passage never suggests that gardening caused her heart attack.

q:
(1) Mercy Valley Hospital should turn the empty lot behind its east wing into a community garden. Patients could see green space from their windows, staff could take breaks outdoors, and the hospital's nutrition program could teach classes using fresh vegetables.

(2) Some board members argue that the lot should be saved for a future parking garage. However, the hospital's own ten-year plan places new parking on the west side of campus, and a garden could be moved in a single season if plans ever changed.

(3) A garden would cost less than $20,000 to build. The board should approve it this spring.

What is the main purpose of paragraph 2?
o: to answer an objection to the author's proposal
to provide evidence that gardens improve patient health
to describe the location of the empty lot on the hospital campus
to summarize the costs and benefits of the garden
w: Paragraph 2 states an opposing view (save the lot for parking) and then rebuts it with the hospital's own plan and the garden's flexibility. Raising and answering an objection is a common purpose of a paragraph in a persuasive text.

n.1: Benefits to patients appear in paragraph 1, and no health evidence is offered anywhere in the passage.
n.2: The lot's location is given in paragraph 1; paragraph 2 mentions campus locations only to rebut the parking argument.
n.3: Cost appears only in paragraph 3, and paragraph 2 does not weigh costs against benefits.

q:
I was twenty-three when I lost my first patient. Mr. Alvarez had told me about his grandchildren every morning for two weeks, and I had promised to see the photos his daughter was bringing on Friday. He died on Thursday night. I followed every step I had been taught: I called the physician, notified the family and prepared the body with care. Then I sat in the supply room and cried. Twenty years later, I still think of him whenever a patient starts to tell me about the people they love.

What is the author's primary purpose in this passage?
o: to persuade hospitals to offer grief counseling to nurses
to express the author's feelings about a past experience
to inform new nurses about the steps to follow after a death
to entertain readers with a suspenseful hospital story
w: The first-person reflection, the detail about the photos and the admission that the author cried and still remembers the patient all show a writer sharing personal feelings. Expressing emotion about an experience is the purpose.

n.0: The passage never mentions counseling or asks hospitals to do anything.
n.2: The steps after a death are mentioned in a single sentence as part of the memory; they are not explained in a way meant to teach.
n.3: The story is moving rather than suspenseful, and it is told to share feelings rather than to amuse or thrill.

q:
Many parents worry that their toddlers are not eating enough vegetables. Children's appetites can change from day to day, and refusing a new food is a normal stage of development. "It can take ten or more tries before a child accepts a new vegetable," says Dr. Maya Thompson, a pediatrician who has studied children's eating habits for fifteen years. Parents can help by serving small portions of new foods next to familiar favorites and by eating the same foods themselves.

Why does the author most likely include the quotation from Dr. Thompson?
o: to support the advice with an expert's credibility
to tell a personal story that appeals to parents' emotions
to introduce a view that the author goes on to argue against
to change the subject from toddlers to older children
w: Dr. Thompson's credentials (a pediatrician with fifteen years of research) lend authority to the claim that repeated tries are normal. Using an expert's standing to support a point is an appeal to credibility, or ethos.

n.1: The quotation states a research-based fact rather than a personal story, and its appeal rests on expertise, not emotion.
n.2: The author agrees with Dr. Thompson; the advice that follows builds on her statement.
n.3: The passage stays focused on toddlers; the quotation is about children accepting new vegetables, the same subject.

q:
Our county's public pools close every year on Labor Day, even though September temperatures here average 88 degrees. According to the county parks report, pool attendance on the last two weekends of August averaged 1,400 swimmers a day. A splash pad, a ground-level area of water jets with no standing water, costs far less to staff than a pool. It is shameful that families with no air conditioning are left with nowhere to cool off. The county must keep at least one pool open through September. Call your commissioner today.

Which features of the passage indicate that its primary purpose is to persuade rather than to inform? Select all that apply.
o: the average September temperature
the instruction to call a commissioner today
the emotionally charged word "shameful"
the demand that the county keep a pool open
the attendance figures from the county parks report
the definition of a splash pad
w: Loaded language ("shameful"), a direct claim about what the county must do and a call to action are features that mark persuasive writing. They show the facts in the passage are being used to push readers toward an action.

n.0: A temperature figure is a neutral fact that could appear in any kind of text.
n.4: Statistics appear in informative and persuasive texts alike; the figures alone do not show the author's purpose.
n.5: Defining a term is a typical feature of informative writing, so the definition does not mark the passage as persuasive.

q:
The blue light from phones and tablets signals the brain to stay awake, and a 2023 survey found that children who used screens in the hour before bed slept 40 minutes less on school nights than children who did not. Tired children struggle to pay attention in class and are more likely to be irritable. Parents, it is time to act. Set a family rule that all screens go into a basket in the kitchen one hour before bedtime, and follow the rule yourselves.

Which of the following best states the author's purpose?
o: to discuss the topic of children's sleep and electronic devices
to report the results of a 2023 survey about children's screen use
to describe a typical bedtime routine in an American family
to convince parents to limit children's screen use before bed
w: The passage builds to direct commands ("Parents, it is time to act. Set a family rule..."), so its purpose is to convince parents to take a specific action.

n.0: This names the topic, not the purpose. It leaves out the author's clear push for a particular action.
n.1: The survey is one piece of supporting evidence; the passage does not report its methods or full results.
n.2: The basket in the kitchen is a recommendation, not a description of what families already do.

q:
Hospitals today spend millions of dollars on hand-hygiene programs, yet studies still find that health care workers clean their hands less than half as often as they should. The idea itself is not new. In 1847, a Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis required doctors at a Vienna maternity clinic to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients, and deaths among new mothers in his ward fell sharply. The challenge today is not knowledge but habit: busy staff forget, skip steps or assume gloves are enough.

The author mentions Ignaz Semmelweis mainly to
o: show that the value of handwashing has been known for a long time.
entertain readers with a story about a famous European doctor.
explain how chlorine solutions kill the germs that cause infection.
persuade readers that modern doctors should study medical history.
w: The sentence just before the example says "The idea itself is not new," and the Semmelweis example from 1847 supports that point. The detail sets up the author's argument that today's problem is habit, not lack of knowledge.

n.1: The example is brief and factual; it serves the author's point about habit rather than amusing the reader.
n.2: The passage says Semmelweis used chlorine but never explains how it works on germs.
n.3: The author never suggests that doctors study history; the example supports a point about hand hygiene.

q:
The Clearwater City Council will vote on June 9 on a plan to place 30 bike-share stations downtown. Riders would pay $2 for a 30-minute trip or $90 for a yearly pass. Supporters, including the downtown business association, say the program would reduce traffic and bring shoppers to Main Street. Opponents, including several residents of the Elm Park neighborhood, worry that the stations would take up 60 parking spaces. A similar program in nearby Fairview has averaged 410 rides a day since it opened in 2022.

What is the primary purpose of the passage?
o: to report on a proposal and the views on both sides
to criticize residents who oppose the bike-share stations
to compare Clearwater's traffic problems with Fairview's
to persuade readers to support the bike-share plan
w: The passage gives the vote date, the prices and the Fairview figures, and it reports both supporters' and opponents' views without taking a side. Balanced reporting of a proposal is an informative purpose.

n.1: Opponents' concerns are presented in neutral terms, with no criticism from the author.
n.2: Fairview appears once as background; the passage says nothing about traffic problems in either city.
n.3: Supporters' arguments are reported, but so are opponents' concerns, and the author never urges a vote either way.

q:
A Nutrition Facts label lists the serving size at the top, followed by the number of calories in one serving. Below that, the label shows nutrients such as fat, sodium and added sugars, along with a Percent Daily Value for each. A Percent Daily Value of 5 percent or less means a food is low in that nutrient, and 20 percent or more means it is high. All of these numbers apply to one serving, so a person who eats two servings must double them.

Which sentence, if added to the end of the passage, would best fit the author's purpose?
o: Percent Daily Values are based on a 2,000-calorie diet for a typical adult.
Food companies make labels confusing so that shoppers will buy more.
I still remember how confused I was the first time I tried to read a label.
Every family should stop buying snacks with more than 10 grams of added sugar.
