w: The passage explains, in a neutral way, how to read the parts of a label, so its purpose is to inform. A sentence adding another factual detail about the label (the 2,000-calorie basis of Percent Daily Values) continues that purpose.

n.1: This accuses companies of a motive without evidence, adding a biased claim that does not match the neutral explanation.
n.2: A personal memory would add an expressive, first-person note to an impersonal explanation.
n.3: This tells families what they should do, which would shift the passage from informing to persuading.

q:
Grayson County Hospital began in 1912 as a six-bed clinic above a hardware store. In 1925, after a fire destroyed the store, the town raised money for a two-story brick building on Elm Street. During the 1950s, the hospital added a maternity ward and its first X-ray machine. A new emergency department opened in 1978, and in 2004 the hospital joined the regional Lakeshore Health network. Today, Grayson County Hospital has 140 beds and employs more than 900 people.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: compare and contrast
cause and effect
problem and solution
chronological order
w: The passage moves through the hospital's history date by date, from 1912 to today. Ordering events by time is chronological structure.

n.0: The passage traces one hospital over time; it does not set two subjects side by side.
n.1: One causal link appears (the fire led to a new building), but the passage as a whole is organized by dates, not by causes and their results.
n.2: No central problem is identified and solved; the passage lists milestones in order.

q:
Oral and tympanic thermometers are both common in clinics. An oral thermometer is placed under the tongue and takes about 10 to 40 seconds to give a reading, depending on the model. A tympanic thermometer, by contrast, reads the temperature inside the ear in one to two seconds. Both give reliable results when used correctly. However, oral readings can be thrown off if a patient has just had a hot or cold drink, whereas tympanic readings can be affected by earwax or a poorly placed probe.

Which organizational structure does the author use?
o: chronological order
description
classification into types
compare and contrast
w: The passage sets two thermometers side by side, noting similarities ("both") and differences ("by contrast," "however," "whereas"). That is compare-and-contrast structure.

n.0: Times appear (seconds per reading), but the passage does not narrate events or steps in order.
n.1: Each thermometer is described, but the descriptions are arranged to show how the two are alike and different, which makes the structure comparative.
n.2: Classification sorts many items into categories; this passage weighs two specific devices against each other.

q:
Last year, patients at Northgate Hospital's emergency department waited an average of 74 minutes before seeing a provider, and nearly one in ten left before being seen. To address this, the hospital made three changes in January. A nurse now assesses each patient at the front door, patients with minor injuries go to a separate fast-track area, and lab tests can be ordered before a patient reaches a room. Since the changes, the average wait has dropped to 31 minutes.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: order of importance
problem and solution
description
compare and contrast
w: The passage opens with a problem (long waits and patients leaving), explains the steps taken "to address this," and reports the result. That is problem-and-solution structure.

n.0: The three changes are listed as equal parts of one plan; none is ranked as most or least important.
n.2: The changes are explained as a response to a problem rather than as features described for their own sake.
n.3: The before-and-after wait times show results, but the passage is built around fixing a problem, not around comparing two subjects.

q:
Using Your Metered-Dose Inhaler

1. Remove the cap and shake the inhaler well for five seconds.
2. Breathe out fully, away from the inhaler.
3. Place the mouthpiece between your teeth and close your lips around it.
4. Press down on the canister once while breathing in slowly and deeply.
5. Hold your breath for 10 seconds, then breathe out slowly.
6. If a second puff is prescribed, wait one minute, shake the inhaler again and repeat steps 2 through 5.
7. If your inhaler contains a steroid, rinse your mouth with water after each use.

Which feature of this text most clearly marks it as technical writing rather than expository writing?
o: It numbers each action the reader must take, in order.
It uses a title that names the subject of the text.
It leaves out opinions and emotional language.
It presents accurate information about a medical device.
w: Technical (procedural) texts give exact, ordered directions for doing a task or using equipment. The numbered commands ("Remove," "Breathe out," "Hold your breath") set this text apart from an expository text, which explains a topic without walking the reader through actions step by step.

n.1: Expository articles also have titles naming their subject, so a title does not identify a text as technical.
n.2: Expository writing is also neutral and free of opinion, so this feature is shared by both types rather than distinguishing them.
n.3: Expository texts also present accurate information, so accuracy does not separate the two types.

q:
Why do so many water mains break in January? Water expands by about 9 percent when it freezes. When the ground around a buried pipe freezes, it shifts and pushes against the pipe, placing stress on joints and older sections. Cold water inside the pipe also makes metal and plastic more brittle. As a result, a pipe that has handled years of normal pressure can crack during a hard freeze. Older cast-iron mains are especially likely to fail because decades of corrosion have already thinned their walls.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: problem and solution
chronological order
classification
cause and effect
w: The passage opens with a "why" question and answers it with causes (freezing, shifting ground, brittleness, corrosion) and their effect (cracked pipes). Signal words such as "as a result" and "because" confirm a cause-and-effect structure.

n.0: The passage explains the breaks but proposes no fix, so it lacks the solution half of this structure.
n.1: The passage explains why something happens, not a series of events in time order.
n.2: Cast-iron mains are singled out once, but the passage does not sort pipes into categories.

q:
Why should healthy adults get a flu shot every fall? Above all, the vaccine lowers your risk of serious illness, hospitalization and death from influenza. It also protects the people around you, including infants and older adults, who are more likely to become seriously ill. In addition, a flu shot can reduce the number of workdays and school days you miss. Finally, and least important for most people, vaccination can spare you a week of feeling miserable on the couch.

How does the author organize the reasons in the passage?
o: in chronological order, from the first event to the last
from the most important reason to the least important
by classifying adults into groups at different risk
by comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated adults
w: "Above all" introduces the strongest reason, and "least important for most people" marks the weakest at the end. Ranking reasons from most to least important is order-of-importance structure.

n.0: "Finally" can signal time order, but here it introduces the last reason in a ranked list, not the last event in a sequence.
n.2: Infants and older adults are mentioned as people who benefit, but the passage does not sort adults into risk categories.
n.3: The passage lists benefits of vaccination; it never describes unvaccinated adults for comparison.

q:
Burns are grouped into types according to how deeply they damage the skin. A superficial burn, often called first-degree, affects only the outer layer of skin and causes redness and pain. A partial-thickness burn, or second-degree burn, reaches into the layer below and usually forms blisters. A full-thickness burn, or third-degree burn, destroys both layers and may look white, brown or leathery. Because nerve endings can be destroyed, a full-thickness burn may cause less pain than a smaller, shallower one.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: classification
chronological order
spatial order
cause and effect
w: The opening sentence says burns are "grouped into types," and the rest of the passage defines each type by its depth. Sorting a subject into categories is classification.

n.1: The types are listed by depth, not in time order; no events unfold.
n.2: Skin layers are mentioned, but the passage is not a description of where things are located in space; it defines categories.
n.3: The last sentence explains one cause and effect (destroyed nerves, less pain), but that detail sits inside the larger classification.

q:
Welcome to the Oakridge Family Clinic. As you enter through the main doors, the check-in desk is directly in front of you. The waiting area lies to your right, with a children's play corner along its far wall. To the left of the check-in desk, a short hallway leads to exam rooms 1 through 6. The lab is at the end of that hallway, across from the restrooms. The pharmacy window is just outside the main doors, to the left of the entrance.

Which organizational structure does the author use?
o: chronological order
order of importance
spatial order
classification
w: The passage locates each area by its position relative to the visitor ("directly in front of you," "to your right," "at the end of that hallway"). Organizing details by location is spatial order.

n.0: "As you enter" sets a starting point, but the passage maps where things are rather than narrating events in time.
n.1: No area is ranked as more or less important; each is placed by location.
n.3: The areas are not sorted into types or categories; they are positioned on a mental map.

q:
Many older adults in Lakeview County miss medical appointments because they no longer drive and the nearest bus stop is more than a mile from the clinic. To fix this, the county launched a ride program last spring. First, a patient calls the clinic at least two days before the visit. Next, a dispatcher schedules a volunteer driver. Then the driver picks the patient up at home and waits during the appointment. In its first six months, the program provided 1,800 rides, and missed appointments fell by a third.

Which of the following best describes the overall organization of the passage?
o: cause and effect, because it explains why patients miss visits
compare and contrast, because it gives results before and after
chronological order, because it lists the steps a patient follows
problem and solution, because it presents a need and a response
w: The passage opens with a problem (missed appointments due to lack of transportation), describes the county's ride program as the fix, and reports its results. The ordered steps and the opening cause are parts of that larger problem-and-solution structure.

n.0: "Because" explains the problem in the first sentence, but most of the passage describes the program created to solve it.
n.1: A drop in missed appointments shows the solution worked; the passage does not set two subjects side by side.
n.2: "First," "next" and "then" order the steps of the solution, but they cover one section, not the passage as a whole.

q:
When a child has a high fever or a deep cut on a Saturday night, parents in Millbrook have two choices. Urgent care centers treat minor injuries and illnesses, such as sprains, ear infections and cuts that need stitches. Visits typically cost less, and waits are often under an hour. Emergency rooms, on the other hand, are equipped for life-threatening problems such as trouble breathing, seizures or severe bleeding. They are open around the clock but usually cost more and can involve longer waits for less serious cases.

The author most likely uses a compare-and-contrast structure in order to
o: show how emergency rooms have changed over the years.
argue that urgent care centers should replace emergency rooms.
help parents decide which place fits a child's needs.
explain what causes most childhood injuries on weekends.
w: Setting the two options side by side (what each treats, cost, wait times, hours) gives parents the information they need to choose between them. The structure serves that practical purpose.

n.0: The passage describes both places as they are now; it gives no history.
n.1: The passage presents emergency rooms as necessary for life-threatening problems, so it does not argue for replacing them.
n.3: Injuries are named as examples of what each place treats; their causes are never discussed.

q:
In 2019, the town of Ridgeway closed its only grocery store. As a result, many residents began buying most of their food at gas stations and dollar stores. Because of the distance to the nearest supermarket, 12 miles away, families without cars ate fewer fresh fruits and vegetables. For example, a survey by the county health department found that produce purchases fell by half. Meanwhile, rates of diabetes in the town continued to rise. In contrast, a neighboring town that kept its grocery store saw little change. The store's closing led to a new effort to start a weekly farmers market.

Which phrases from the passage signal a cause-and-effect relationship? Select all that apply.
o: Meanwhile
In contrast
Because of
led to
For example
As a result
w: "As a result" introduces an effect of the closing, "Because of" introduces a cause of the change in eating habits, and "led to" links the closing to the farmers market effort. All three signal cause and effect.

n.0: "Meanwhile" signals that two things happened at the same time, a time relationship rather than a causal one.
n.1: "In contrast" signals a difference between two towns, which is a compare-and-contrast signal.
n.4: "For example" introduces supporting evidence (the survey), not a cause or effect.

q:
We reached the trailhead at dawn, our breath fogging in the cold. By noon we had climbed above 11,000 feet, and my sister Leah said she felt dizzy and had a pounding headache. I remembered from our guidebook that altitude sickness often appears above 8,000 feet and that the safest treatment is to go back down. We turned around without reaching the summit. By the time we reached the lake at 9,500 feet, Leah's headache had eased, and we ate our sandwiches on a rock, watching the clouds drift over the peak we had left behind.

Which type of text is this passage?
o: narrative
technical
expository
persuasive
w: The passage tells a first-person story with characters, a setting and events in order (the climb, Leah's symptoms, the decision to turn back). That makes it a narrative.

n.1: No step-by-step instructions are given; the guidebook detail is remembered, not presented as directions.
n.2: The passage includes a fact about altitude sickness, but that fact is part of the story; the text as a whole recounts an experience rather than explaining a topic.
n.3: The narrator never argues for a position or urges the reader to act.

q:
The night before my first clinical shift, I laid out my scrubs, packed my stethoscope and set three alarms. When I walked onto the unit at 6:45 a.m., the charge nurse looked up from her computer. "You must be the new student," she said. "You'll be with Marcus today. Stick close to him, ask questions, and don't touch any pumps unless he says so." I nodded and tried to look calmer than I felt. My hands were shaking as I followed Marcus down the hall.

From which point of view is the passage narrated?
o: third person omniscient
third person limited
first person
second person
w: The narrator takes part in the events and refers to herself as "I" and "my" throughout. That is first-person narration.

n.0: An omniscient narrator reports every character's thoughts; this narrator reports only her own feelings and what others say aloud.
n.1: A third-person narrator stands outside the story and uses "he" or "she" for the main character; this narrator is the main character.
n.3: "You" appears only inside the charge nurse's dialogue. Pronouns in quoted speech do not set the narrator's point of view.

q:
Dr. Nadia Hassan studied the X-ray for a long moment. She was almost sure the fracture would need surgery, but she wanted the orthopedic team to confirm it before she said anything to the family. In the waiting room, Mr. Brooks paced between the vending machine and the window, checking his phone every few seconds. His daughter sat with her arm in a sling, staring at the floor. When Dr. Hassan finally walked in, she smiled and said, "Let's talk about next steps."

Which point of view does the author use in the passage?
o: first person
third person omniscient
third person limited
third person objective
w: The narrator uses "she" and reports Dr. Hassan's private thoughts (she was almost sure about surgery, she wanted confirmation). Mr. Brooks and his daughter are shown only through their actions. Access to one character's mind is third person limited.

n.0: The narrator never says "I"; the only first-person words would be in dialogue, and there are none.
n.1: An omniscient narrator would reveal what Mr. Brooks and his daughter were thinking. Here we see only their actions.
n.3: An objective narrator reports only actions and speech, but this narrator tells us Dr. Hassan's thoughts.

q:
Coach Rivera paced the sideline, certain that his team had one more good play left in them. On the bench, Tyler rubbed his sore ankle and hoped the coach would not notice, because he wanted desperately to finish the game. In the stands, Tyler's mother gripped her program and wondered whether she should have let him play at all. And the referee, who had made a questionable call in the first half, quietly promised himself that he would get the next one right.

Which point of view does the author use?
o: third person objective
first person, told by an observer
third person limited
third person omniscient
w: The narrator stands outside the story and reveals the private thoughts of four different people: the coach, Tyler, his mother and the referee. Knowing the minds of many characters is third person omniscient.

n.0: An objective narrator reports only what can be seen and heard, but this narrator tells us what each person hopes, wonders and promises privately.
n.1: No narrator refers to himself or herself as "I," not even an onlooker; every character is described from outside.
n.2: A limited narrator reveals one character's thoughts; this one moves freely among several.

q:
As a pharmacist for twenty years, I have watched patients struggle to open childproof medicine caps. Those caps have saved countless children from accidental poisonings, and I would never want them removed from homes with young children. But many of my older customers have arthritis, and some of them leave their bottles open on the counter because they cannot reopen them. Federal rules already allow patients to request easy-open caps. Pharmacies should make that choice clear to every customer over sixty-five who lives without children.

Which of the following best describes the author's point of view on childproof caps?
o: They should be removed from all prescription bottles.
They are useful but should be optional for some patients.
They are a federal requirement that pharmacies cannot change.
They have failed to prevent accidental poisonings in children.
w: The author praises the caps for protecting children yet argues that older adults without children at home should be clearly offered easy-open caps. The view is balanced: keep the caps, but make the alternative known.

n.0: The author says the caps should not be removed from homes with young children, so this goes too far.
n.2: The author notes that federal rules already allow patients to request easy-open caps, so the caps are not an unchangeable requirement.
n.3: The author says the opposite: the caps "have saved countless children."

q:
Opponents of the city's plan to put calorie counts on restaurant menus argue that diners do not read them and that the signs will only raise costs for small businesses. It is true that calorie labels alone will not solve obesity. But a 2018 study of a large restaurant chain found that customers ordered about 4 percent fewer calories after labels appeared, and many restaurants quietly made their dishes lighter. Those small changes add up across millions of meals. The council should pass the measure.

With which statement would the author most likely agree?
o: Calorie labels offer small benefits that add up over time.
Most diners do not read calorie counts printed on menus.
Calorie labels are not worth the cost to small businesses.
Calorie labels by themselves can solve the problem of obesity.
w: The author argues that a 4 percent reduction and lighter recipes "add up across millions of meals" and urges the council to pass the measure. Small but meaningful benefits sum up the author's view.

n.1: This is the opponents' claim, which the author reports in order to rebut it. A view the author reports is not necessarily the author's own.
n.2: This is also the opponents' argument; the author supports the measure despite the cost concern.
n.3: The author concedes that labels "alone will not solve obesity," so the author would reject this claim.

q:
The so-called wellness program at Harmon Industries is a disaster. Fewer than 22 percent of employees signed up last year, and the company paid a consulting firm $180,000 to run it. Workers were bombarded with nagging emails about step counts, and the heavily promoted health screenings drew only 140 people out of 2,300. Anyone who thinks this program is helping employees has not been paying attention.

Which of the following best describes the passage?
o: It is objective, because it is written in the third person.
It is subjective, because it is written from the employees' view.
It is objective, because its claims are based on numbers.
It is subjective, because its word choice shows a clear slant.
w: The statistics are factual, but "so-called," "disaster," "bombarded" and "nagging" reveal the author's negative judgment. Slanted word choice makes a text subjective even when it includes numbers.

n.0: Third-person writing can be subjective; this passage uses third person yet clearly argues a judgment.
n.1: The passage is subjective, but not because of whose view it reflects; the author never says employees share this view. The slanted wording is what makes it subjective.
n.2: Statistics do not make a text neutral. The author selects and frames the numbers with loaded language to support a strong opinion.

q:
Since the new staffing rules took effect, each nurse on our unit has cared for no more than five patients per shift, down from seven. I finally have time to explain a new medication properly, to notice when a patient's breathing changes, and to eat lunch sitting down. Management keeps talking about the cost of hiring more staff. They are not the ones running between rooms at 3 a.m. when two call lights go off at once.

The author of the passage is most likely
o: a reporter writing a news story about staffing rules.
a hospital administrator reviewing the cost of new staff.
a patient who was recently treated on the unit.
a nurse who works shifts on the unit.
w: The author refers to "our unit," describes caring for patients and explaining medications, and contrasts the writer's own night-shift experience with management's view. These details point to a staff nurse's perspective.

n.0: A news reporter would write in a neutral voice, but this author writes from personal, first-hand experience.
n.1: The author criticizes management for focusing on cost, which is the opposite of an administrator's perspective.
n.2: The author describes caring for several patients at once, which a patient would not do.

q:
You wake at 4:30 a.m., before the alarm, because your body has learned the schedule. You pull on scrubs in the dark so you will not wake anyone, grab the lunch you packed last night and drive through empty streets to the hospital. By 6:45 you are taking report from the night nurse, and by 7:15 you have already answered three call lights. Your feet ache by noon. Still, when a patient squeezes your hand and thanks you, you remember why you chose this work.

From which point of view is the passage written?
o: first person
third person limited
third person objective
second person
w: The narration addresses the reader directly as "you" and places the reader in the role of the nurse. That is second-person point of view.

n.0: The passage reads like a personal memory, but no "I" or "we" appears; every action is assigned to "you."
n.1: Third-person limited would describe a character as "he" or "she" and reveal that character's thoughts.
n.2: Third-person objective would describe characters from outside using "he" or "she," reporting only actions and speech.

q:
The bus pulled up to the clinic at 8:02. A woman in a red coat stepped off first, holding a toddler on her hip. She walked to the front desk and set down a folder. "We have a nine o'clock with Dr. Lee," she said. The receptionist glanced at the clock, then at the folder. "You're early," she said. "Have a seat." The woman sat down by the window. The toddler pressed his hand against the glass and watched the bus pull away.

Which point of view does the author use?
o: third person limited
first person
third person omniscient
third person objective
w: The narrator reports only what could be seen and heard (arrivals, movements and dialogue) and never reveals any character's thoughts or feelings. That is third-person objective.

n.0: A limited narrator would reveal one character's thoughts, such as why the woman came early; none are given.
n.1: "We" and "you" appear only inside the dialogue. The narrator never speaks as "I."
n.2: An omniscient narrator would reveal several characters' thoughts; this narrator reveals none.

q:
Our school district's plan to give every high school student a free tablet has real promise. Students without computers at home would finally be able to complete online assignments, and teachers could share lessons more easily. Still, I have questions. The district has not explained who will repair broken devices, and it has budgeted no money for training teachers to use them well. If those gaps are filled before the fall, I will be among the plan's strongest supporters.

Which of the following best describes the author's attitude toward the tablet plan?
o: opposed, with a few exceptions
supportive, with reservations
enthusiastic, with no concerns
neutral, with no stated view
w: The author praises the plan's "real promise" but raises questions about repairs and training, and promises full support only if those gaps are filled. Support with conditions is a qualified, or cautiously supportive, attitude.

n.0: The author's main stance is favorable; the concerns are conditions for full support, not reasons to oppose the plan.
n.2: The author raises two specific concerns, so the support is not unqualified.
n.3: The author clearly expresses a view ("real promise," "I have questions"), so the passage is not neutral.

q:
The county's proposal to close the Pine Street library branch, which opened in 1964, has drawn strong reactions. The county manager calls the branch "an expensive relic in the age of e-books." Several council members argue that the money would be better spent on road repairs. But the branch is the only place in the neighborhood with free internet access, and I see seniors there every day filling out benefit forms they cannot complete at home. Closing it would cut off people who have no other option. The county should find savings elsewhere.

Which statements from the passage express the author's own point of view? Select all that apply.
o: The Pine Street branch opened in 1964.
The proposal to close the branch has drawn strong reactions.
The money would be better spent on road repairs.
Closing it would cut off people who have no other option.
The branch is an expensive relic in the age of e-books.
The county should find savings elsewhere.
w: In the author's own sentences, the author judges that closing the branch would harm people with no alternative and concludes that the county should find savings elsewhere. These two statements express the author's position in favor of keeping the branch.

n.0: The opening date is a checkable background fact; it expresses no judgment about the proposal.
n.1: This is a neutral report that people have reacted strongly; it takes no side and does not state the author's own position.
n.2: This is the argument of several council members, which the author reports but does not share.
n.4: These are the county manager's words, quoted by the author in order to argue against them.

q:
The Brookside Health Fair drew about 600 visitors to the community center on Saturday. Nurses from three local clinics offered free blood pressure checks, and a dentist handed out toothbrushes to children. Organizers called the event "our best fair yet" and plan to hold it again next spring. Sadly, the fair's single diabetes screening table could not keep up with the line. Dozens of people left without being tested, some after waiting more than an hour.

Which sentence from the passage most clearly reveals the author's perspective?
o: Nurses from three local clinics offered free blood pressure checks.
Organizers called the event "our best fair yet" and plan to hold it again next spring.
Dozens of people left without being tested, some after waiting more than an hour.
Sadly, the fair's single diabetes screening table could not keep up with the line.
w: "Sadly" is the author's own reaction, and it shows concern that the fair fell short in an important area. The other sentences report events or quote someone else without the author adding a judgment.

n.0: This neutrally reports a service that was offered.
n.1: "Our best fair yet" is a judgment, but it is the organizers' view, which the author quotes. A view the author reports is not the author's own perspective.
n.2: This sentence supports the author's concern, but it reports a checkable outcome without any judgment word; it does not state the author's attitude as clearly as "Sadly" does.
